questions.q: According to this lesson, why does a company-wide SRE mandate tend to fail in an organization that has no existing SRE practice?
options: It reads as more process with no demonstrated payoff and meets predictable resistance, since there's no shared vocabulary or track record yet
SRE practices are only legally required for companies above a certain size
SLOs cannot be defined unless every team adopts them simultaneously
Error budgets only function correctly when applied company-wide on day one
questions.explain: Announcing a top-down initiative into an organization with no existing SRE vocabulary or results reads as pure process overhead, which is exactly the resistance a pilot is designed to avoid.

questions.q: What three properties make a service a good candidate for an SRE pilot?
options: The newest service in the company, built by the most junior team, with no current users
Business-critical enough to matter, owned by one team willing to try something new, and already has acknowledged operational pain
A service with zero incidents in its history, so there is nothing to measure
Any service chosen at random to keep the process fair across teams
questions.explain: A good pilot service is important enough that improvement is visible, has a willing owning team, and has real, already-acknowledged pain — so a measurable improvement gets noticed.

questions.q: The lesson argues that defining an SLO and error budget IS the pilot, not a step before it. What does that mean in practice?
options: The SLO only needs to be written down in a document; using it is optional during the pilot
The error budget should be calculated only after the pilot period ends
The pilot team must run its real work — deploys, on-call, prioritization — against the error budget during the measurement period, or the SLO is just a document, not a practice
SLOs are a replacement for having a pilot at all
questions.explain: An SLO that never actually changes a real decision, like pausing a risky deploy, is paperwork. The pilot only counts as real SRE practice if the error budget is actually used to make decisions.

questions.q: What makes a pilot's results convincing enough that another team will want to adopt SRE practice voluntarily?
options: A slide deck describing SRE theory, independent of any specific team's results
A mandate from leadership announced after the pilot concludes
The pilot team's headcount increasing during the trial

Before-and-after numbers (incident frequency, detection/resolution time, decisions actually changed by the error budget) plus the pilot team's own account of the experience, including that they'd recommend it
questions.explain: Metrics alone aren't enough if the team hated the process; a pilot that improved results and that the team would recommend to a peer is what turns adoption into a request instead of a mandate.

questions.q: Why would a pilot on a service nobody cares about fail to make the case for wider SRE adoption, even if the metrics technically improved?
options: Because no one was watching that service, so a measurable improvement there doesn't get noticed or build any organizational case for expanding the practice
Because low-visibility services are not permitted to have SLOs
Because SLOs cannot mathematically be calculated for low-traffic services
Because error budgets require a minimum number of daily users to function at all
questions.explain: A pilot's persuasive power comes from visible, acknowledged improvement. A service nobody was paying attention to proves nothing to the rest of the organization even if its numbers improved.
